notable_claims: A UofI sysadmin claimed the University steps in if language is vulgar or rude to a 'reasonable person'.
The 1985 University Code states students are free from institutional censorship and that campus press/media should be free of censorship.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie questions whether the University of Illinois's free speech policies apply to computer media after a system administrator suggested that vulgar or rude language could trigger university intervention. Kadie cites the University Code (1985) regarding freedom from institutional censorship and references legal precedents from the University of Michigan and University of Wisconsin.
classification.title: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

identity.subject: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

notable_claims: The University of Illinois may intervene if language is vulgar or rude to a 'reasonable person'.
There was a dispute over whether the Daily Illini accurately quoted university administration regarding speech restrictions.
classification.summary: A discussion among students and staff at the University of Illinois regarding a Daily Illini report on university speech restrictions. The thread focuses on a statement attributed to sysadmin Bob Foertsch suggesting that the University intervenes when language is deemed vulgar or rude to a 'reasonable person.' Participants express surprise and debate whether such restrictions contradict existing free speech policies.
classification.title: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

identity.subject: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

notable_claims: A student's account was disabled by university administration after posting critical and aggressive comments about a computer company head.
Sharp tone or lack of decorum does not strip speech of First Amendment or academic freedom protections.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a report from John Hascall regarding the suspension of a student's account after the student posted that a computer company executive 'should be dead'. Kadie argues against the punishment, citing ACLU principles and academic freedom to defend sharp or strident speech.
classification.title: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

identity.subject: Re: Watch What You Post!!! (1984 Revisited)

notable_claims: Iowa State University policy forbade 'rude' speech and messages of a political nature on electronic mail or bulletin boards.
The EFF provided legal resources arguing that public university rules against harassment may be struck down if they are too broad or vague (citing Doe v. University of Michigan).
Campus mail systems may be classified as limited public forums under the Public Forum Doctrine.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie of the EFF responds to a discussion regarding Iowa State University's computer policy, which prohibited 'rude, obscene or harassing material' and messages of a 'commercial or political nature.' Kadie questions the authority and vagueness of these restrictions and provides a curated reading list of legal precedents concerning free expression at public universities. The exchange highlights early conflicts between university acceptable use policies (AUPs) and First Amendment rights on campus networks.
classification.title: Iowa State speech restrictions

identity.subject: Iowa State speech restrictions (was Re: Watch What You Post!!!)

notable_claims: There is no established procedure for appealing computer expulsion from ACS.
The lack of a formal appeal process may be used to argue that computer expulsions are not 'disciplinary' actions.
organizations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (implied by uiuc.edu)
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the lack of formal appeal procedures for students and faculty expelled from Academic Computing Services (ACS) computers. He argues that the absence of a defined process violates principles of student rights and freedoms by leaving users without recourse. Kadie highlights a potential logical loop where computer expulsions are not classified as disciplinary actions, thereby exempting them from standard disciplinary appeal processes.
classification.title: Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

identity.subject: Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

notable_claims: Brack claims his only impactful action was using a 'fixman' command that caused no permanent damage.
Brack asserts he was not informed of the rules he allegedly violated until after the actions occurred.
The dispute highlights a conflict between administrative authority and the need for written, public computer use policies.
classification.summary: Steven S. Brack responds to criticisms regarding his expulsion from Ohio State University (OSU) for computer-related offenses. Brack argues that the university overreacted to minor incidents, specifically a command that removed underlining from man pages, and claims he was punished based on non-public rules.
classification.title: Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

identity.subject: Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

notable_claims: Rice University required permission for off-campus mail to ensure users read the Appropriate Use policy and that usage was connected to education.
The university's restrictive policies were a response to two lawsuits involving forged emails sent by a student.
System administrators advised against disabling 'talk' messages to avoid misinterpreting user activity during suspicious events.
classification.summary: Joseph A. Watters defends Rice University's 'Appropriate Use of Computer Facilities' policy against claims that it is draconian. He explains that requirements for permission to send off-campus mail were implemented following lawsuits involving a student who forged emails. The discussion highlights the tension between university liability management and user autonomy on early campus networks.
classification.title: Re: Rice University's Owlnet and University Computing Policies

identity.subject: [comp.admin.policy]  Re: Rice University's Owlnet and University Computing Policies

notable_claims: The owner of Odyssey dropped screening to avoid the risk of lawsuits that could shut down a small operation.
Prodigy faced complaints from the ADL regarding its failure to screen content effectively.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie reports that Odyssey, a commercial Bulletin Board System (BBS) in California, has ceased its practice of screening and censoring content. The owner cited the risk of lawsuits as a primary motivator, referencing legal pressures faced by Prodigy from the ADL. The owner claimed previous censorship was primarily focused on maintaining topic relevance rather than making value judgments.
classification.title: A Commercial BBS drops screening/censoring

notable_claims: U.S. District Judge E.B. Haltom ruled that Alabama A&M students must be informed of specific charges and witness names during disciplinary proceedings.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares a report from the Birmingham News regarding a ruling by U.S. District Judge E.B. Haltom. The judge ruled that students facing disciplinary action at Alabama A&M University must be informed of specific charges and provided with the names of witnesses testifying against them.
classification.title: Due process at Alabama A&M

notable_claims: Restrictive system policies at Toledo were attributed to a single unpleasant experience with an undergraduate user years prior.
Administrative favoritism occurred at OSU where MUD games were permitted because a sysadmin was one of the users.
The authors argue that mutual respect and dialogue between admins and users are more effective than ultimatums for maintaining system stability.
classification.summary: A discussion between system administrators regarding the balance of authority and user relations in academic computing environments. The participants contrast a restrictive administrative culture at Ohio State University with a more open, educational approach used at other institutions. They discuss specific incidents involving printer misuse and MUD (Multi-User Dungeon) gaming as catalysts for policy enforcement.
classification.title: Re: [comp.admin.policy] Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

identity.subject: Re: [comp.admin.policy]  Re: Re; Brack Expulsion. What Happened?

notable_claims: Better communication between users and admins can avoid most conflicts.
Reducing bureaucratic layers between users and administrators could save money.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur proposes methods to reduce conflict between computer users and system administrators. He suggests lowering user-to-administrator ratios, limiting total users per system, and removing bureaucratic layers to allow direct communication.
classification.title: User/admin communication

notable_claims: Acceptable Use policies are overly restrictive because they imply that anything not explicitly permitted is forbidden.
Over-regulation of computing freedom could negatively impact the US software industry.
Most resource consumption problems result from user ignorance rather than malice and can be solved through education and direct communication.
classification.summary: Vincent Fox critiques the rise of 'Acceptable Use' policies at universities, arguing that they stifle computing freedom by requiring permission for any activity not explicitly listed as acceptable. He proposes replacing these restrictive policies with a list of 'Unacceptable Uses' and focusing on user education and direct management of resource abuse. Fox suggests that system administrators should prioritize making the user community aware and free rather than relying on bureaucratic legislation.
classification.title: "Acceptable Use" Policies. Why does everyone want one?

identity.subject: [comp.org.eff.talk]  "Acceptable Use" Policies. Why does everyone want one?

notable_claims: The finger utility was invented in 1972 at the Stanford A.I. Lab.
The original design of finger did not include a mechanism for users to remain anonymous.
classification.summary: Les Earnest, the creator of the finger utility, acknowledges that the program lacks a feature for user anonymity. He notes that he developed the tool in 1972 as a local utility for the Stanford A.I. Lab before it was expanded for network access.
classification.title: Re: Finger & Liberty
